prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "CVS HEALTH Corp" (ticker CVS). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:

   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: CVS Health is a well-known incumbent in mature industries, not a Rule Breaker: its revenue grows in single digits, its advantage is shared with rivals such as UnitedHealth and Cigna, and its stock is up only about 21% over five years. It fails Gardner's tests for an emerging industry, a beloved brand and a hard-to-copy edge.
summaries.buffett: CVS is a large, understandable franchise with steady revenue growth (to $402.1 billion in 2025) and a cheap forward P/E near 11.5, but operating income fell from $13.9 billion in 2020 to $4.7 billion in 2025, debt is $61.4 billion and returns on capital are low. Buffett would find the moat narrow and the earnings record too inconsistent for a high-conviction holding.
summaries.munger: Inverting, there are several ways CVS can disappoint: PBM reform, government rate pressure on Aetna, litigation and a shrinking retail pharmacy. It is a fair business at a low price rather than the great business Munger preferred.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify CVS as a turnaround stalwart: adjusted EPS is guided to rise from $6.75 to $7.90-$8.10 in 2026 and the forward P/E is about 11.5. But GAAP results are volatile, insiders are not buying and the share count is creeping up, so it only partly fits.
summaries.fisher: CVS is adding products (Cordavis biosimilars, AI tools for claims and call centers, Oak Street primary care), but margins have fallen for years and its care-delivery bets needed a $5.7 billion impairment in 2025. It falls short of Fisher's standard of sustained above-average growth and widening margins.
summaries.graham: CVS is large, pays a long-running dividend and trades at about 1.5 times book, but it lost money in 2018, GAAP EPS fell from $6.44 in 2017 to $1.39 in 2025, and its trailing P/E of about 24 fails Graham's price tests.
summaries.thiel: CVS is a scale incumbent in a regulated oligopoly without a ten-times-better technology or a secret; it scores on distribution (about 9,000 stores, 87 million PBM members) but poorly on Thiel's questions about technology, monopoly and unique insight.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would note the rebounding earnings, a 2026 adjusted EPS guide raised twice and a free-cash-flow yield near 7%, but low revenue growth (about 3-4% expected for 2026) and heavy debt make it a value recovery rather than a durable growth compounder.
summaries.druckenmiller: The change at the margin is positive: Aetna's medical benefit ratio improved from 89.9% to 87.4% year over year in Q2 2026 and guidance was raised. Policy risk to PBMs and Medicare Advantage, and a falling share price since July, argue against a large concentrated bet.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high margins and low debt; CVS has a 1.2% operating margin in 2025, returns on equity in the mid single digits and $61.4 billion of debt, so it does not fit his quality test despite a low price.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, trailing operating profit of about $8.3 billion gives an earnings yield near 5% on a $166 billion enterprise value, and return on tangible capital is weighed down by debt and $85.5 billion of goodwill, so it would rank as middling.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, able and honest management and reinvestment runway; CVS has experienced management and scale, but its returns are low and its reinvestment in care delivery has destroyed value, so it fits poorly.
summaries.pabrai: CVS looks like Pabrai's temporarily troubled business: the price fell to about $53 (adjusted) in late 2024 when Aetna's costs spiked, and recovery is underway. At $92.36 much of the easy upside is gone and the debt load raises downside risk, so the heads-I-win odds are less compelling.
summaries.wood: CVS is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's platforms; it is an incumbent that digital pharmacies and AI-driven health-care startups aim to disrupt, so it does not fit Cathie Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions; CVS generates cash (about $7.8 billion of free cash flow in 2025) and is dominant in pharmacy and PBMs, but its earnings are exposed to government policy and have been unpredictable.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model would require CVS to pass savings to customers and grow ever stronger; CVS's rebate-based PBM model is under attack for doing the opposite, and its position is not clearly strengthening, so it fits poorly.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge markets and companies solving painful problems at their start; drug costs and health coverage are huge, painful problems, but CVS is a mature incumbent rather than an early-stage disruptor.
summaries.nash: CVS fails most of Nash's hard filters: revenue growth below 10%, an operating margin near 1-2%, debt far above cash and major regulatory threats. Its Nash scorecard totals about 50, well below the 75 threshold, and Nash's DCF at 12% gives about $66 a share against $92.36.

momentum.evidence: The shares rose about 21% over the year to $92.36 on Oct 16, 2026 (from about $76 adjusted in October 2025), ahead of the S&P 500, but they are down from a 52-week high of $110.68 and fell after the August Q2 report.

g4.evidence: Chairman and CEO David Joyner is an experienced PBM executive and Glenview Capital founder Larry Robbins sits on the board, but Robbins sold 378,000 shares in May 2026 and there is no famous long-term backer like Berkshire.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly see CVS as undervalued: 27 analysts rate it a Strong Buy with an average target of $115.48, 25% above the $92.36 price, at about 11.5 times 2026 adjusted EPS.

simple.evidence: The pieces (drugstores, health insurance, drug benefits) are familiar, but PBM rebates, medical-cost reserving and government reimbursement rules make profits hard for a generalist to forecast, as the 2024 Aetna surprise showed.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $268.7 billion in 2020 to $402.1 billion in 2025, but GAAP diluted EPS swung from $5.46 (2020) to $6.47 (2023), $3.66 (2024) and $1.39 (2025), and there was a net loss in 2018.

integrity.evidence: Management has been candid about Aetna's problems and has raised guidance, but CVS has paid large legal settlements (Omnicare False Claims Act and opioid charges in 2025) and replaced its CEO in October 2024 after earnings disappointments.

b6.evidence: CVS built its integrated model through large acquisitions (Aetna in 2018, Signify Health and Oak Street Health in 2023), and the care-delivery deals led to a $5.7 billion goodwill impairment in 2025.

roic.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $8.3 billion on roughly $127 billion of equity plus net debt is about a 6.5% pre-tax return, with $61.4 billion of debt.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capex) was $7.8 billion in 2025, far above $1.8 billion of net income, and 2026 operating cash flow is guided to at least $11.5 billion.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings and debt funded acquisitions such as Oak Street and Signify, yet operating income fell from $13.9 billion in 2020 to $4.7 billion in 2025 and the share price is about where it was in 2021.

safety.evidence: At about 11.5 times 2026 consensus adjusted EPS of $8.04 the stock looks cheap, but Nash-style DCF on actual 2023-2025 free-cash-flow margins (about 2.2%) gives roughly $66 a share at 12%, so the margin of safety depends on earnings recovery.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E near 11.5, a 2.9% dividend yield and about a 6.6% free-cash-flow yield on 2025 FCF are reasonable for a mature, recovering business.

mu5.evidence: Ways to fail include PBM reform, Medicare Advantage rate cuts, client losses (Caremark claims fell from 2.3 billion in 2023 to 1.9 billion in 2025), retail pharmacy decline, litigation and high debt.

reinvest.evidence: Recent reinvestment into care delivery earned poor returns (a $5.7 billion impairment in 2025 and Oak Street clinic closures planned for 2026), and the core businesses are mature.

ly2.evidence: It fits Lynch's turnaround category: Aetna margin recovery drove adjusted EPS from $5.42 in 2024 to $6.75 in 2025 and a guided $7.90-$8.10 in 2026.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 11.5 is below 2026's expected adjusted EPS growth of about 19%, but above the 6% growth consensus expects for 2027, and the trailing GAAP P/E is about 24.

runway.evidence: An ageing population and rising drug spending (US dispensing revenue up 10% in 2025 to $751 billion) support growth, but consensus sees only about 3.7% a year revenue growth to 2028.

ly7.evidence: Insiders are not buying (May 2026 open-market sales by director Larry Robbins and EVP Tilak Mandadi), and diluted shares rose from 1,262 million in 2024 to 1,287 million in Q2 2026.

ly8.evidence: CVS is a widely followed mega-cap covered by about 27 analysts, not an overlooked niche.

fi2.evidence: As retail pharmacy matures, management has pushed into primary care, biosimilars (Cordavis) and AI tools such as Aetna's Claims Assist Manager, though results have been mixed.

fi3.evidence: CVS does not report R&D spending as a separate line, and the payoff of its technology investments is not yet measurable.

fi4.evidence: Its sales organisation wins large PBM and employer contracts and Aetna kept more than 69% of MA members in 4-star-plus plans, but Caremark lost claims volume in 2024 and 2025.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in AI and care delivery, but recent priorities have been near-term margin repair: exiting the ACA exchanges, closing stores and cutting benefits.

gr1.evidence: CVS had $402.1 billion of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $118 billion.

ni10.evidence: CVS reported a net loss of $594 million in 2018 after a $6.1 billion goodwill impairment on its long-term care business.

gr4.evidence: CVS has paid dividends without interruption for decades (Bullfincher counts 42 continuous dividend years); the quarterly dividend is $0.665.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS was $1.39 in 2025 against $6.44 in 2017 and $5.46 in 2020, far from a one-third rise.

gr6.evidence: The 2023-2025 average GAAP EPS of about $3.84 puts the $92.36 price at about 24 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E near 24 times a price-to-book near 1.5 gives about 36, above 22.5.

th1.evidence: CVS has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; Express Scripts and Optum Rx run comparable PBM platforms.

timing.evidence: Demographics and GLP-1 drug demand favour pharmacy and Medicare businesses now, but policy timing is unfavourable, with PBM reform and Medicare Advantage rate pressure.

th3.evidence: CVS is already a leader in very large markets (about 26% of US PBM claims, 12% of Medicare Advantage), not a company expanding from a small niche.

team.evidence: Management is experienced (Joyner has 37 years in health care and PBM), but it is not a founder-led or exceptional team, and the previous CEO was replaced in 2024.

th5.evidence: Distribution is its strength: about 9,000 stores, more than 800 MinuteClinics, 87 million Caremark members and over 37 million Aetna members.

durable.evidence: People will still need drugs and coverage in 20 years and CVS's scale should endure, but PBM economics and retail pharmacy face structural pressure from reform and online rivals.

th7.evidence: Integrating pharmacy, PBM and insurance is a strategy also pursued by UnitedHealth, Cigna and Humana, not a unique insight.

trend.evidence: CVS benefits from ageing and drug spending but is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift such as AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Adjusted EPS rose from $1.81 to $2.58 in Q2 2026 and full-year guidance was raised twice in 2026, to $7.90-$8.10.

dr2.evidence: Continued Aetna margin recovery could make results look better by 2028, but consensus already expects 2026 EPS of $8.04 and only about 6% growth in 2027.

dr4.evidence: Health care demand is resilient in a slowdown, but CVS's $61.4 billion of debt makes it sensitive to interest rates and its insurance margins to government rate decisions.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on Nov 4, 2026, 2027 Medicare Advantage repricing with Aetna's strong 2027 Star ratings, and possible 2027 guidance are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Policy, litigation and medical-cost risks are too high for a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: After cost of products ($221.2B) and health care costs ($125.5B), only about 13.8% of 2025 revenue was left, and the operating margin was 1.2%.

fcfyield.evidence: 2025 free cash flow of $7.8 billion is about a 6.6% yield on a roughly $118.9 billion market value, attractive for a mature, recovering company.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $8.3 billion is about 5% of an enterprise value near $166 billion, moderate rather than high.

pa2.evidence: Aetna's 2024 medical-cost spike was a fixable pricing problem; the medical benefit ratio fell from 89.9% in Q2 2025 to 87.4% in Q2 2026 after repricing and exits.

pa4.evidence: CVS is cash-generative and essential, which limits permanent loss, but $61.4 billion of debt and policy risk to PBMs mean permanent impairment cannot be ruled out.

wo1.evidence: CVS uses AI in call centers and claims processing but is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its costs are not falling quickly with volume; it is a mature pharmacy, PBM and insurance business.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Consensus expects revenue to grow from $402.1 billion to about $448 billion by 2028, not many-fold.

ac3.evidence: It does not depend on commodity prices, but its results depend on government reimbursement rates, drug pricing policy and interest rates on $61.4 billion of debt.

ns1.evidence: PBMs are criticised for keeping rebate and spread savings rather than passing them on, and CVS's model is under regulatory pressure on exactly that point.

ns4.evidence: Scale and Aetna's quality ratings should keep it a leader, but PBM reform, online pharmacy and transparent-pricing rivals make a clearly stronger position in 10-20 years uncertain.

va2.evidence: It addresses the large, painful problem of access to and cost of medicines and health coverage for tens of millions of Americans.

tn1.evidence: CVS sells into ageing and drug-spending trends but as an old pharmacy and insurance business, not a company built for a secular technology trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees CVS as a drugstore-plus-insurer-plus-PBM in recovery, which is what it is; there is no hidden transformation.

tn3.evidence: It is a $118 billion US company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue has grown every year since 2020 and it is profitable ($1.8 billion of 2025 net income), but debt of $61.4 billion far exceeds $14.0 billion of cash, with no infrastructure-type reason for the miss.

tn5.evidence: Operating cash flow has been positive (six-month 2026 OCF $10.6 billion), but cash ($14.0 billion at June 2026) has been far below debt ($61.4 billion) every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 7.8% in 2025 and management guides to about 3% growth in 2026 (at least $414.0 billion).

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 7.8% plus a 2025 free-cash-flow margin of 1.9% is about 10, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In the first half of 2026 revenue rose 6.7% to $206.5 billion while operating income rose from $5.8 billion to $9.4 billion, so expenses grew more slowly than revenue.

tn9.evidence: It hits several instant kills: debt far above cash, an operating margin near 1-2% (well below 20%) and revenue growth below 10% and slowing.

tn10.evidence: PBM reform proposals, FTC scrutiny of PBM rebating, Medicare Advantage policy and ongoing opioid and False Claims Act litigation are major regulatory and legal threats.

tn11.evidence: CVS provides pharmacies, drug-benefit management and health insurance that help employers, governments and patients get affordable medicines and care, and it charges dispensing margins, PBM fees and rebate spreads, and insurance premiums.

tn13.evidence: Total about 50: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 0, short interest (1.3%) 10, institutional ownership (about 92%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 0.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year 2020-2025, but operating margin fell from 5.2% to 1.2%, free cash flow fell from $13.4 billion to $7.8 billion and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: 2025 operating income of $4,660M covered $3,119M of interest only 1.5 times, assets excluding goodwill ($168.3B) are below liabilities ($173.9B), and the current ratio is 0.87 at June 2026, though liabilities are only 2.2 times equity.

tn18.evidence: Joyner has led a successful margin recovery since October 2024, but he has made no open-market share purchases and has been CEO for two years, not ten, and is not a founder.

tn20.evidence: CVS has beaten adjusted EPS estimates for at least five straight quarters, including Q2 2026 ($2.58 vs about $1.85 expected).

tn21.evidence: Margins have declined for years (operating margin 5.2% in 2020 to 1.2% in 2025) and CVS has a record of large acquisitions (Aetna, Signify, Oak Street) followed by impairments.

tn22.evidence: CVS has $402 billion of revenue, positive cash flow and no habit of issuing shares to raise cash, so it is far from a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At a 2.2% average free-cash-flow margin and 7.7% growth, Nash's DCF yields about $66 at 12%, so the $92.36 price implies higher margins or growth than CVS has recently delivered.

tn25.evidence: Using 2023-2025 averages (7.7% revenue growth, 2.2% FCF margin), 4% terminal growth, $14.0B cash and $61.4B debt, value is about $66 a share at 12% (about $101 at 10%) versus $92.36.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E near 11.5 is low versus peers and the PEG on 2026's roughly 19% adjusted EPS growth is about 0.6, but on 2027's expected 6% growth the PEG is about 1.9.
